topics/configuration-of-3-planes.title: Configuration of 3 planes
topics/configuration-of-3-planes.content:
Vocabulary
A system of linear equations is consistent if it has at least one solution.
A system is inconsistent if it has no solutions.
Possible Configurations
Assuming all three planes are distinct, there are five possible configurations.
1. Three Parallel Planes
No plane intersects any other plane.
No solutions.
2. Two Parallel Planes Cut by a Third Plane
Two planes are parallel and the third intersects both.
No solutions.
3. Three Planes Intersect at a Point
All three planes share exactly one common point.
One unique solution.
4. Sheaf of Planes
All three planes contain the same line.
Infinitely many solutions.
The common line consists entirely of points satisfying all three equations.
5. Triangular Prism Configuration
Each pair of planes intersects in a line, but there is no point common to all three planes.

The Tests
Determining the Configuration
Suppose the planes are
a_1x+b_1y+c_1z=d_1
a_2x+b_2y+c_2z=d_2
a_3x+b_3y+c_3z=d_3
The following tests should be carried out in order.
Test 1: Check for Parallel Planes
Two planes are parallel if the left-hand sides are scalar multiples.
If both sides are multiplied by the same scalar, the equations represent the same plane.
For example,
6x-3y+6z&=2\end{align}$$

are parallel planes.

$$\begin{align} 4x - 2y + 4z &= 5 \\ 8x - 4y + 8z &=10 \end{align}$$

describe the same plane.

> [!important]  
> 
> If Test 1 identifies parallel planes, the configuration must be either:
> 
> - Three parallel planes
> - Two parallel planes cut by a third plane

No further tests are required.

### 2. Check if the determinant is non-zero
Consider the system of linear equations written as a matrix equation
$$\begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix}$$
If the coefficient matrix
$$A=\begin{pmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3\end{pmatrix} $$
is such that
$$det(A)\neq0$$
then the matrix is non-singular and has an inverse.

The system can be solved by
$$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix}$$
Since an invertible matrix always gives a unique solution,

> [!important]  
> 
> A non-zero determinant implies the three planes intersect at a single point.

### 3. Test for consistency
If we reach this stage, then:
- no planes are parallel (Test 1)
- $\det(A)=0$ (Test 2)

Therefore the configuration must be either:
- a **sheaf** (infinitely many solutions), or
- a **triangular prism** (no solutions).

Reduce 3 equations in 3 unknowns to 2 equations in 2 unknowns:

$$\begin{aligned} p_1 x + q_1 y &= r_1 \\
p_2 x + q_2 y &= r_2 \end{aligned}$$

Since $\det(A)=0$, these equations cannot intersect at a unique point.

Therefore only two possibilities remain:

- the lines are identical;
- the lines are parallel.

##### Case 1: Identical Lines

Manipulate both equations so that the left-hand sides are identical.
If the right-hand sides are also identical, the equations represent the same line.
Hence there are infinitely many solutions.

> [!important]  
> 
> The planes form a **sheaf**.

##### Case 2: Parallel Lines

Manipulate both equations so that the left-hand sides are identical.
If the right-hand sides are different, the equations represent parallel lines.
Hence there are no solutions.

> [!important]  
> 
> The planes form a **triangular prism**.

topics/determinant-of-a-2-by-2-matrix.title: Determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix
topics/determinant-of-a-2-by-2-matrix.content:
Definition
For a matrix
M=  
\begin{pmatrix}  
a & b \\ 
c & d  
\end{pmatrix}  
the determinant of M is defined as


                  
                  Important
                  
                

\det(M)=\begin{vmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc



Geometric Interpretation
The determinant measures the area scale factor of the transformation represented by the matrix.
If a shape has area A, then after transformation by matrix M its new area becomes:
|\det(M)|\times A  

Why the Absolute Value Appears
Area itself cannot be negative, so we use:
|\det(M)|  
for the area scale factor.
However, the sign of the determinant still contains important geometric information.

Effect of a Negative Determinant
If:
\det(M)<0  
then the transformation reverses orientation.
Geometrically this means the transformation includes a reflection.

Orientation Change
For example:

clockwise ordering may become anticlockwise
a shape may become “flipped”


Determinant Equal to Zero
If:
\det(M)=0  
the transformation squashes the plane into a lower dimension.
Examples include:

flattening the plane onto a line
collapsing everything to a single point.


Singular Matrices
A matrix with determinant zero is called a singular matrix.


                  
                  Important
                  
                

Singular matrices do not have inverses.



Why No Inverse Exists
When a transformation squashes space into a lower dimension, information is lost.
Different input vectors may produce the same output vector.
This creates a many-to-one mapping.

Example
Consider:
M=  
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 0 \\ 
0 & 0  
\end{pmatrix}  
Then:
M  
\begin{pmatrix}  
x \\ 
y  
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}  
x \\ 
0  
\end{pmatrix}  
All points with the same x-coordinate map to the same image.
For example:
\begin{pmatrix}  
3 \\ 
1  
\end{pmatrix}  
,  
\qquad  
\begin{pmatrix}  
3 \\ 
100  
\end{pmatrix}  
both map to:
\begin{pmatrix}  
3 \\ 
0  
\end{pmatrix}  
The original vector therefore cannot be recovered uniquely.
So an inverse transformation cannot exist.

Key Summary





















DeterminantGeometric Meaning\det(M)>0Area scaled, orientation preserved\det(M)<0Area scaled, orientation reversed\det(M)=0Space collapsed into lower dimension.

topics/direction-cosines.title: Direction cosines
topics/direction-cosines.content:
Direction Cosines are not a new idea, they are a language of something you already know: a unit vector.
Consider a unit vector \begin{pmatrix} l \\ m \\ n \end{pmatrix}.
There are two things we know:

l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1
\begin{pmatrix} l \\ m \\ n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\alpha \\ \cos\beta \\ \cos\gamma \end{pmatrix}
where \alpha, \beta and \gamma are the angles the vector makes with the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis respectively.

Problem solving with direction cosines

topics/direction-ratios.title: Direction ratios
topics/direction-ratios.content:
Direction ratios are a convenient way of describing the direction of a line.
For example, the vector \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} has direction ratios 3:-2:5
To find the direction cosines of a vector, turn it into a unit vector first.

topics/equality-of-matrices.title: Equality of matrices
topics/equality-of-matrices.content:
Equality of Matrices


                  
                  Definition
                  
                

Two matrices A and B of the same order m \times n are equal, A = B, if and only if
A_{ij} = B_{ij}
\quad \text{for all } 1 \le i \le m,\; 1 \le j \le n.


Example
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & -2 & 3 \\
0 & 4 & 5
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
B =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & -2 & 3 \\
0 & 4 & 5
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
C =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & -2 & 3 \\
0 & 4 & 6
\end{pmatrix}.


A = B (all entries match).


A \ne C because A_{2,3} = 5 but C_{2,3} = 6.



Solving a Simple Matrix Equation
\underbrace{
\begin{pmatrix}
x^2 & 5x - 6 \\
5   & 8-x
\end{pmatrix}
}_{A}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{pmatrix}
5x - 6 & 2x \\
5      & x+4
\end{pmatrix}
}_{B}


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Equating corresponding elements
\begin{aligned}
&\quad x^2 = 5x - 6
&&\Longrightarrow x=2 \text{ or } 3, \\
&\quad 5x - 6 = 2x
&&\Longrightarrow x=2, \\
&\quad 5 = 5
&&\text{(always true)}, \\
&\quad 8-x = x+4
&&\Longrightarrow x=2.
\end{aligned}


Conclusion: Both x=2 and x=3 satisfy the first equation, but only x=2 satisfies all equations.
Hence the unique solution is
\boxed{x=2}.

topics/integration-by-substitution-(inde.title: Integration by substitution (indefinite)
topics/integration-by-substitution-(inde.content:
Write out the integral
\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{\ln x}{x(1+\ln x)^2}}\text{ d}x
Change what you are integrating with respect to
\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{\ln x}{x(1+\ln x)^2}}\dfrac{\text{ d}x}{\text{ d}u}\text{ d}u
Use the substitution given to find the derivative;
differentiate as is.
\begin{align}
u&=1+\ln x\\
\dfrac{\text{ d}u}{\text{ d}x}&=\dfrac{1}{x}\\
\dfrac{\text{ d}x}{\text{ d}u}&=x
\end{align}

Substitute as is into integral:
\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{\ln x}{x(1+\ln x)^2}}x\text{ d}u
Simplify if it does:
\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}}\text{ d}u
Complete the substitution:
\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{u-1}{u^2}}\text{ d}u
Integrate:
&=\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{1}{u}}-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\text{ d}u\\
&= \ln |u| + \dfrac{1}{u} + c
\end{aligned}$$

Reverse the substitution:
=\ln|1+\ln x| + \dfrac{1}{1+\ln x}+c

topics/iteration.title: Iteration
topics/iteration.content:
We use fixed point iteration to solve equations of the form
\text{f}(x)=0
by rearranging into the form
x=\text{g}(x)
A root occurs when a value of x satisfies this equation. This value is called a fixed point.
Method


Rearrange the equation
Rewrite \text{f}(x)=0 in the form
x=\text{g}(x)
Note: Different rearrangements give different iteration functions and may not all converge.


Choose a suitable starting value
Pick an initial value x_0 close to the expected root (usually given to you).


Apply the iteration process
Use the rule
x_{n+1}=\text{g}(x_n)
to generate successive approximations:
x_1, x_2, x_3, ...


Check for convergence
The method is converging if the values settle towards a single number.


Staircase and Cobweb Diagrams

topics/l'hôpital's-rule.title: L'Hôpital's rule
topics/l'hôpital's-rule.content:
L’Hôpital’s Rule is used to evaluate limits that produce the indeterminate forms
\frac{0}{0} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.
If f(x) and g(x) are differentiable near x=a, and
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 \text{ and } \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0
or
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \pm\infty \text{ and } \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \pm\infty,
then, provided the limit on the right hand side exists,
\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}
=
\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}.
Conditions

f and g must be differentiable near a
g'(x) \neq 0 near a
The original limit must give 0/0 or \infty/\infty
The limit of \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} must exist (or be infinite)

Method

Substitute the limit value.
Check that the result is 0/0 or \infty/\infty.
Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately.
Evaluate the new limit.
Repeat if necessary.

Proof of L’Hôpital’s rule

topics/locating-roots-in-a-given-interva.title: Locating roots in a given interval
topics/locating-roots-in-a-given-interva.content:
To show that an equation of the form f(x)=0 has at least one root in the interval [a,b]:
The formal result (Intermediate Value Theorem)
If a function f(x) is continuous on the interval [a,b], and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then there exists at least one root \alpha such that  a < \alpha < b
In plain English, this works because a continuous graph must cross the x-axis when moving from a positive value to a negative value.
However, if there is no sign change, this does not rule out the existence of a root.
Example
\ln x - \dfrac{1}{x} = 0
Note that the RHS is zero, so the equation is in the correct form.
Observe that:
\text{f}(1.5)=-0.261...
\text{f}(2)=0.193...
Since \text{f} is continuous over the interval [1.5,2] and there is a sign change, then there exists a root, \alpha, such that 1.5<\alpha<2

topics/matrices---vocabulary-and-notatio.title: Matrices - vocabulary and notation
topics/matrices---vocabulary-and-notatio.content:
Key Vocabulary & Notation


Matrix: a rectangular array of elements (numbers) in rows and columns.


Notation: denoted by a capital letter, e.g. A, B, M. Brackets are mandatory:


A =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6
\end{pmatrix}.


Order (size): “rows \times columns”.
A 2 \times 3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns.



Key Vocabulary & Notation


Square matrix: order n \times n.
E.g. 2 \times 2, 3 \times 3.


A =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 \\
-4 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.

Zero matrix: all entries zero, denoted \mathbf{0}_{m \times n}.

A =
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.

Identity matrix: square with 1’s on the main diagonal and 0’s elsewhere, denoted \mathbf{I}_n.

I_3 =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.

topics/matrices-as-linear-transformation.title: Matrices as linear transformations
topics/matrices-as-linear-transformation.content:
Matrices can be used to represent linear transformations of the plane.
A matrix acts on a vector and transforms it into another vector.
Geometrically, this means matrices can:

stretch
reflect
rotate
shear

points in the coordinate plane.

Transforming a Single Point
A point in the plane is represented by its position vector.
For example:
\mathbf{v}
=
\begin{pmatrix}  
2 \\  
1  
\end{pmatrix}  
Suppose the transformation matrix is
A=  
\begin{pmatrix}  
2 & 1 \\  
0 & 1  
\end{pmatrix}  
Then the image of the point is found by matrix multiplication:
A\mathbf{v} =

\begin{pmatrix}  
2 & 1 \\  
0 & 1  
\end{pmatrix}  
\begin{pmatrix}  
2 \\  
1  
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}  
5 \\  
1  
\end{pmatrix}  
So the point (2,1) is transformed to (5,1).

Transforming Multiple Points Simultaneously
Several position vectors can be transformed at once by placing them into a single rectangular matrix.
Suppose the vertices of a shape are:
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 \\  
1  
\end{pmatrix},  
\qquad  
\begin{pmatrix}  
2 \\  
1  
\end{pmatrix},  
\qquad  
\begin{pmatrix}  
2 \\  
3  
\end{pmatrix}  
These can be written together as:
P=  
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 2 & 2 \\ 
1 & 1 & 3  
\end{pmatrix}  
Applying the transformation:
AP
= \begin{pmatrix}  
2 & 1 \\ 
0 & 1  
\end{pmatrix}  
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 2 & 2 \\ 
1 & 1 & 3  
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}  
3 & 5 & 7 \\ 
1 & 1 & 3  
\end{pmatrix}  
Each column of the resulting matrix gives the image of the corresponding point.

Important Properties of Linear Transformations
Linear transformations preserve important geometric structure.
1. The Origin is Invariant
All linear transformations leave the origin fixed.
Since:
A  
\begin{pmatrix}  
0 \\ 
0  
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}  
0 \\ 
0  
\end{pmatrix}  
the origin never moves.

2. Straight Lines are Preserved
Linear transformations map straight lines to straight lines.
For example, a square may become a parallelogram but straight edges remain straight.

Degenerate Cases
If the determinant is zero, an entire line may collapse to a point or a shape may collapse to a line or a point.
For example:
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 0 \\ 
0 & 0  
\end{pmatrix}  
squashes the plane onto the x-axis.

3. Parallel Lines are Preserved
Parallel lines remain parallel after a linear transformation.
Again, degenerate cases may cause them to collapse onto the same line or point.

4. Equally Spaced Points Remain Equally Spaced
If points divide a line segment into equal intervals before the transformation, they still do afterwards.
This happens because linear transformations preserve ratios along lines.

Key Idea


                  
                  Important
                  
                

Linear transformations preserve geometric structure while changing geometric appearance.

topics/matrix-multiplication-laws.title: Matrix multiplication laws
topics/matrix-multiplication-laws.content:
1. Commutative?


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.


For matrices:
AB \ne BA

Simple Demonstration
Consider:
A =  
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 2 & 3 \\  
4 & 5 & 6  
\end{pmatrix}  
and
B =  
\begin{pmatrix}  
1 & 2 \\ 
3 & 4 \\ 
5 & 6  
\end{pmatrix}  
Then:

AB gives a 2\times2 matrix
BA gives a 3\times3 matrix
Since the resulting matrices have different sizes, they cannot possibly be equal.


2. Associative Law
Matrix multiplication is associative.
(AB)C = A(BC)  

Connection to Functions
For functions:
(\text{f} \text{g}) \text{h} = \text{f} (\text{g} \text{h})  
Matrices behave in the same way because matrix multiplication represents composition of linear transformations, which are a special type of function.

3. Compatibility with Scalar Multiplication
Matrix multiplication is compatible with scalar multiplication.
k(AB) = (kA)B = A(kB)  
where k is a scalar.


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Nearly every algebraic structure we meet in this course behaves this way.



4. Distributive Law
Matrix multiplication distributes over addition.
Left distributive law
A(B+C) = AB + AC  
Right distributive law
(A+B)C = AC + BC  


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Nearly every algebraic structure we meet in this course behaves this way.



Key Summary

























PropertyTrue for matrices?Commutative❌ NoAssociative✅ YesCompatible with scalar multiplication✅ YesDistributive over addition✅ Yes



                  
                  Exam tip
                  
                

The most common mistake is assuming:
AB = BA  
This is usually false. Order matters in matrix multiplication.

topics/negation-examples.title: Negation examples
topics/negation-examples.content:
1. Universal statement
Statement:
All even integers are divisible by 2.
Negation:
There exists an even integer that is not divisible by 2.

2. Universal with inequality
Statement:
For all real numbers x,   x^2 \geq 0.
Negation:
There exists a real number x such that x^2 < 0

3. Existential statement
Statement:
There exists a prime number that is even.
Negation:
No prime number is even.

4. Existential with restriction
Statement:
There exists a real number x such that x^2 = 2
Negation:
For all real numbers x,   x^2 \ne 2

5. Conditional statement
Statement:
If an integer is divisible by 4, then it is even.
Negation:
There exists an integer that is divisible by 4 and is not even.

6. Conditional with inequality
Statement:
If x > 2, then x^2 > 4
Negation:
There exists a real number x such that x > 2 and x^2 \le 4

7. Conditional with structure
Statement:
If a number is rational, then its decimal expansion is terminating or recurring.
Negation:
There exists a rational number whose decimal expansion is neither terminating nor recurring.

8. Biconditional statement
Statement:
An integer n is even if and only if n^2 is even.
Negation:
Either there exists an even integer whose square is odd,
or there exists an odd integer whose square is even.

9. Universal conditional
Statement:
For all integers n, if n is odd then n^2 is odd.
Negation:
There exists an integer n such that n is odd and n^2 is even.

10. Statement suited to proof by contradiction
Statement:
\sqrt{2} is irrational.
Negation:
\sqrt{2} is rational.

topics/negation-of-a-statement.title: Negation of a statement
topics/negation-of-a-statement.content:
The negation of a statement is the statement that is true when the original statement is false, and false when the original statement is true.

both statements cannot be true
both statement cannot be false
exactly one statement is true

Standard Patterns
The negation of all … have a property X is there exists a … that does not have property X
The negation of there exists a … which has property X is there are no … which have property X
The negation of “If P then Q” is “P is true and Q is false.”
For example,

“If x is even, then x^2 is even”
Negation: “x is even and x^2 is odd”

Negation examples

topics/numerical-methods.title: Numerical Methods
topics/numerical-methods.content:
A numerical method is a procedure or algorithm used to obtain an approximate solution to a problem where an exact solution is difficult, impossible, or impractical to find algebraically.
Numerical methods are judged by how quickly they converge to a solution, how reliable they are in reaching that solution, and how easy they are to apply. Different methods are suited to different types of problems, so the best method depends on the situation.
1. Speed of convergence

How quickly the method gets close to the true solution
Fewer steps means less work and less rounding error

2. Reliability (likelihood of success)

Whether the method is guaranteed to work
Some methods can fail depending on the starting value

Comparison chart:

topics/problem-solving-with-direction-co.content:
Abstract Problems
Simply substitute what you know into the two relationships concerning direction cosines and solve any relationships it generates.
Contextual Problems
Vectors that are given in modulus argument form, (i.e. those where the magnitude of a vector is given and the angles it makes with the coordinate axes) can be quickly turned into Cartesian vectors. This gives us access to all the vector techniques we know.

topics/proof-by-contradiction.title: Proof by contradiction
topics/proof-by-contradiction.content:
A proof by contradiction has the following four stages:

Assume the negation
Make some deductions based on the negation
Reach a contradiction
State a conclusion

Examples
Proof of irrationality
Proof of the infinitude of primes

topics/proof-of-irrationality.title: Proof of irrationality
topics/proof-of-irrationality.content:
Prove \sqrt{5} is irrational.
Assume \sqrt{5} is rational.

Let \sqrt{5}=\dfrac{a}{b} where a,b\in\mathbb{R} and b\ne0
Also assume that a and b have no common factor greater than 1.

\sqrt{5}&=\dfrac{a}{b}\\
5&=\dfrac{a^2}{b^2}\\
5b^2&=a^2
\end{align*}

\therefore a^2 is a multiple of 5.
\therefore a is a multiple of 5.
Hence a = 5n, where n\in\mathbb{Z}
So,

5b^2 &= (5n)^2\\
5b^2 &= 25n^2\\
b^2 &=5n^2
\end{align*}

\therefore  b^2 is a multiple of 5.
\therefore b is a multiple of 5.
Hence a and b have a common factor of 5.


This contradicts the assumption that a and b have no common factor greater than 1.
Hence, the original statement is true.     \square

topics/proof-of-the-infinitude-of-primes.title: Proof of the infinitude of primes
topics/proof-of-the-infinitude-of-primes.content:
Claim
There are infinitely many prime numbers.
Assume, that there are only finitely many primes.
Then we can list them all as
p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots, p_n.
Now consider the number
N = p_1 p_2 p_3 \cdots p_n + 1.
For each prime p_i in our list, when N is divided by p_i, the remainder is 1.
So no prime in our list divides N
Since N > 1, it must have at least one prime divisor, say q.
This prime q cannot be any of p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n, because none of those primes divides N.
This contradicts the assumption that p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n were all the primes.
\therefore the original statement is true. \square

topics/volume-of-revolution.title: Volume of revolution
topics/volume-of-revolution.content:
General approach to finding area and volumes
Formulae
Volume of revolution about the x-axis:
\int^{x=b}_{x=a} \pi y^2 \text{d}x
parametric formula
\color{red}\int^{t=b}_{t=a} \pi y^2 \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\text{d}t
Volume of revolution about the y-axis:
\int^{y=b}_{y=a} \pi x^2 \text{d}y
parametric formula
\color{red}\int^{t=b}_{t=a} \pi x^2 \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\text{d}t
Cylinders
A cylinder is formed when a line segment parallel to the axis of rotation is rotated about that axis.
i.e.

a horizontal line segment rotated about the x-axis,
or a vertical line segment rotated about the y-axis.

Take care to distinguish clearly between:

the radius, measured perpendicular to the axis of rotation,
and the height, measured parallel to the axis of rotation.

Cones
A cone is formed by rotating an oblique line segment about an axis, where one endpoint of the segment lies on the axis of rotation.
Once again, take care not to confuse:

the radius of the base,
with the perpendicular height of the cone.

The volume of a cone is
V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h
Frustums
If the oblique line segment does not touch the axis of rotation, the resulting solid is a frustum.
Although there is a formula for the volume of a frustum, in questions involving volumes of revolution it is often more reliable to use integration directly rather than memorising another formula.
Symmetrical Curves
If a curve is symmetrical about the axis of rotation and the question asks for a rotation through 180^\circ, simplify the problem. Discard one half of the curve and rotate the remaining half through a full 360^\circ.
General Notes


Integrate in the increasing direction of the variable being used.
This usually means:

left to right when integrating with respect to x,
or bottom to top when integrating with respect to y.



Volumes of revolution should never be negative.
Even if the curve lies below the axis or on both sides of the axis of rotation, the resulting volume must still be positive.
